Hi Jeevan bhai,
Quick update. You told me to stop skimming fifty job posts and read three properly. So I picked three junior backend postings, from a logistics company, a small software firm and a hospital-software company. I copied their skill lists into a sheet and counted repeats: Python in all three, SQL in all three, REST APIs in all three, Docker in two, cloud basics in two. I already know Python and some SQL, so my real gaps are REST APIs and Docker. That is a much cleaner list than get better at coding. My plan before graduation: build one small API project, run it in a container and put it on my resume. Can I send you the project link when it is ready?
Thanks,
Arnab

subtype: Approach: working backward from a target role and its listed skills [Thinking]
passage: Jeevan, you asked how I decided what to learn in final year. Honestly, I stopped guessing. I'm Mridul. In July I picked three real job ads for junior backend developers, from three different companies, and printed them. Then I took a highlighter and marked every skill. Some came up once: one wanted a particular cloud certificate, one wanted a payments background. But three things came up in all of them: databases, building APIs, and version control while working in a team. I could do basic database queries. I had never built an API anyone else used, and my version control was just "save and pray." So I worked backward from graduation in May: an API project by December, version control properly on a classmate's shared project by February, database practice all along. The once-only stuff, I let go. It felt strange to ignore things, but the highlighter made it obvious.

qa.q: How many job postings did Mridul print?
How did Mridul feel about letting go of the once-only skills?
qa.a: Mridul felt a little strange and uneasy ignoring them, but relieved that the highlighter made the priorities obvious.

qa.q: What else could Mridul do to check the plan?
qa.a: Mridul could show the gap list to a senior already working in backend, who might spot a skill the postings take for granted.

qa.q: How might Jeevan see Mridul's method?
qa.a: Jeevan, who asked how Mridul chose, might see a simple method to copy: collect real postings, mark the repeats and plan backward from graduation.

grounding: Shows a final-year student comparing three junior backend postings, listing the skills they repeat, and planning backward to close the biggest gaps.

passage: From my bed in our hostel room, I watched Kunal and Sabina tape three printed job ads to the cupboard door. All three were for junior backend developers. Sabina read aloud while Kunal made tally marks on a sheet. "Databases. Tally. APIs. Tally. Cloud basics. Tally. Testing. Tally." After twenty minutes the sheet showed four skills that came up in every ad and a long tail that came up once. Kunal tapped the sheet. "Databases, I'm fine. Testing, I've never done. APIs, one small project. Cloud, nothing." Sabina said, "So testing and cloud first. You have five months." He wrote two lines in his planner, and under them, "Ignore the once-only ones." I couldn't tell if he was worried or relieved. He went to bed early, which he never does.

qa.q: How many skills came up in every ad?
qa.a: Four skills came up in every ad.

qa.q: How might Kunal have felt reading his gaps aloud?
qa.a: Kunal may have felt worried about the missing testing and cloud skills and relieved to have a clear list, though the roommate couldn't tell which.

qa.q: What else could Kunal do with the five months?
qa.a: Kunal could build one small project that uses testing and a cloud setup together, so both gaps are practised in something he can show.

qa.q: How does the roommate see the evening?
qa.a: The roommate notices the method and Kunal going to bed early, reading it as a sign the plan affected him, without knowing the exact feeling.
